name: Bahamas
summary_text: The Bahamas decriminalised consensual same-sex conduct on 16 May 1991 through the Sexual Offences and Domestic Violence Act. Nothing in the sources indicates that a visitor can be prosecuted for consensual sexual conduct.  The criminal law retains an unequal age of consent. The sources record 16 years for opposite-sex acts and 18 years for same-sex acts.  Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not legal. The Marriage Act defines marriage as between a man and a woman, maritime marriage law provides that a marriage is void if between two men or two women, and in 2011 former Minister of State Zhivargo Laing stated that a same-sex marriage is void as a community standard. Former Prime Minister Perry Christie stated in 2013 that he did not support same-sex marriage and in 2016 that a referendum would not legalize it, defining marriage as between a male and a female determined at birth. Same-sex households are denied the rights accorded to opposite-sex married couples.  The Constitution prohibition on discrimination does not cover sexual orientation or gender identity. The 2006 Constitutional Reform Commission did not regard sexual orientation as deserving of protection, and efforts to include it in a proposed constitution were blocked by members citing religious opposition.  No broad anti-discrimination or anti-harassment law covers sexual orientation or gender identity. Discrimination on those grounds in employment, education, housing, healthcare, banking and public businesses is not illegal, including discrimination in healthcare or education. There are no national hate-crime laws addressing violence directed at lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender people.  Official statements evidence hostility toward transgender people. Government member Leslie Miller publicly called for the exile of transgender people from the Bahamas, denounced the growing transgender community, urged financial contributions to relocate transgender people to a private island to ensure they stay out of the way, and pledged $1,000 toward relocation.  A gay visitor was violently targeted during a major tourist event. On 8 May 2017 The Tribune reported that Adrian Brown, aged 24, born in Jamaica and resident in the United States, was treated at Doctors Hospital for a head laceration after being targeted and beaten because he is gay at Bahamas Junkanoo Carnival early on Saturday, and that he sought charges.  Lethal violence against gay men has resulted in acquittals and unsolved cases. A defendant who killed a homosexual HIV-positive man in 2009 was acquitted after invoking a gay-panic defence. On 10 June 2010 the president of the Court of Appeal stated that a person is entitled to use whatever force is necessary to prevent being the victim of a homosexual act. The accused in the 2007 killing of Harl Taylor was found not guilty. Nine murders of gay men between 2001 and 2015 remain unsolved.  Police action and public protest have affected lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender social life and tourism. Police raided a gay party in downtown Nassau on 6 October 2007 but made no arrests because no crime had been committed, and the Ministry of Tourism later apologized to the cruise company. Church groups protested lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender tourist groups, including opposition to a 2004 cruise associated with Rosie O'Donnell and a 1998 protest against a lesbian cruise. No exclusively gay bars or clubs exist, the Nassau scene is underground, and groups are often pressured to keep social events hidden. In 2016 the Canadian government issued travel advice warning gay couples about the risk of homophobia in the Bahamas.  Social conditions indicate a high level of disapproval. Many Bahamians belong to conservative Christian denominations that treat homosexuality and cross-dressing as decadence and immorality, and politicians have been reluctant to support lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender rights legislation publicly. Surveys recorded 85.5 percent strongly disapproving of same-sex marriage in 2015 with 10.6 percent approving, and over 84 percent strongly disapproving of a gay or lesbian politician in 2013 with 12 percent positive. Due to lack of confidence in the judicial system, legal inequality and homophobia, many lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender people keep sexual orientation or gender identity private.

name: Saint Barthélemy
summary_text: Saint Barthélemy stands under the national framework of France. Criminal law, rules on identity documents, the anti-discrimination statute and the marriage regime apply here as they do in metropolitan France.  Same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised. Private same-sex relations were removed from criminal liability by the Penal Code of 1791 and remained absent from the Penal Code of 1810 as applied in French colonies. The unequal age of consent introduced in 1942 was equalised at 15 on 4 August 1982.  Since 1 January 2017, under the law signed on 18 November 2016, a transgender person can obtain legal change of gender without sex reassignment surgery, sterilisation, psychiatric certificates or medical diagnosis. The application must go before a court. Change of first name can be made separately at the registry office. Non-binary identity is not recognised in French law, so a visitor whose documents record a non-binary marker has no legal counterpart on arrival.  Discrimination on the basis of sexual identity was prohibited in July 2012. The term was replaced by gender identity in Penal Code article 225-1 and in the Labour Code by the law of 18 November 2016. Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation in employment, housing and access to goods and services was prohibited in 1985. The law of 31 December 2004 made homophobic comments punishable by a maximum of 45,000 euro fine and 12 months imprisonment and increased penalties where physical assault or murder was motivated by the sexual orientation of the victim. Since 2017 transphobia constitutes an aggravating circumstance for all crimes punishable by prison.  Same-sex marriage is legal in Saint Barthélemy. It was approved by the National Assembly on 12 February 2013 and the Senate on 12 April 2013, ruled constitutional on 17 May 2013 and signed on 18 May 2013, with the first ceremony held on 29 May 2013. Joint adoption by same-sex couples has been legal since May 2013.  Conversion practices are prohibited. The Senate voted on 7 December 2020, the National Assembly concurred on 25 January 2022 and the ban was published on 1 February 2022. The stated penalty is two years imprisonment and a 30,000 euro fine.  Gender-affirming hormone therapy and surgery are covered by the French framework. One source dates availability to 1975 and another dates domestic legalisation of surgery to 1979. In 2010 France removed gender identity disorder as a diagnosis by decree. Access on the island itself is reported as limited. A 2022 ILGA-Europe report recorded lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and inequitable geographic access for gender-affirming healthcare in France. A visitor requiring such care should expect to rely on provision outside Saint Barthélemy.  Detention falls under the French system. Reporting on that system by the controller-general of detention places finds that trans detainees, overwhelmingly women held under birth-sex placement, suffer the most in prison and that administration policy recognises only biological sex. A 2011 case in Nantes resulted in placement of a trans woman in a men’s prison. The opinion of 25 May 2021 on transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty, based on about 40 referrals since 2010, found that serious violations of fundamental rights persist across places of detention. Its recommendations were stated to apply also to intersex and non-binary persons.  The social environment described for visitors is open and accepting. The luxury-yacht economy has long welcomed gay couples. Same-sex couples are reported to attract no attention and no hostility is noted. Discretion is described as the norm among a high-end visitor population. There are no LGBTQ venues or visible scene and no Pride-specific events. Hotel staff are described as trained for diverse guests.
